Diagonalizable vs. Non-Diagonalizable Matrices
?

There is a theorem that states the following:

If is a matrix, then it is diagonalizable if and only if there exists a basis of that consists of eigenvectors of

We can break this down into two possible cases:

  • If has two distinct eigenvalues, then it is indeed diagonalizable. This is because two distinct eigenvalues will give rise to two linearly independent eigenvectors (one for each eigenvalue).

    So, for a matrix with eigenvalues and and corresponding eigenvectors and we have

  • If we get a double root of the characteristic equation, the matrix will be diagonalizable only if we can find exactly two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to which may or may not be possible. Another way of saying this is that the corresponding eigenspace must be of dimension

So, the eigenvalues are λ1=λ2=1. Since we get one repeated eigenvalue, the matrix might not be diagonalizable. To check this, we row-reduce the matrix (A−1I)x=0:

A−1I=[−23−34]−[1001]=[−33−33]R2:=R2−R1∼[−3300]

Uniqueness of the Diagonalization
?

Given a matrix the diagonalization

is almost unique, but not quite.

When we construct the diagonal matrix we can put the eigenvalues in any order. So this matrix is unique up to permutations of the order of the eigenvalues. Note that by swapping the eigenvalues in we then have to swap the corresponding eigenvectors (columns) in

Also, since any non-zero multiple of an eigenvector is an eigenvector as well, the eigenvector basis of can consist of these multiples instead. So the invertible matrix is unique up to multiples of its columns.
